Serbia woke to a new era on Monday after Mr. Vucic, a frequent visitor to Moscow who had been prime minister or president since 2014, suffered a defeat on Sunday that prompted nationwide celebrations, although few had any idea of how the Balkan country’s new student-backed leaders would govern. Russia saw Mr. Vucic’s Serbia as a crucial ally in Europe, and as a bulwark against what Moscow has cast as the European Union’s aggressive attempts to contain and punish it over its war in Ukraine. Serbia buys large quantities of gas from Russian energy giant Gazprom, and although it has aspirations to join the European Union, it has not signed up to EU-backed sanctions on Russia over Ukraine. Instead, under Mr. Vucic — who enjoyed close ties to President Vladimir Putin — it continued to develop close economic, political and military links to Moscow. The Kremlin put a brave face on Mr. Vucic’s defeat, saying it had taken note of the result and that Mr. Vucic — whose contribution to bilateral ties it warmly praised — was moving into opposition. “As for the new political force that will come to power as a result of the elections, we wish to express our hope that its actions will also be constructively directed towards the further development of relations, and that these new political forces will understand that cooperation with Russia is in Serbia’s interests, because it benefits Serbia,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said. “For our part, we intend to continue to do everything we can to foster the development of our relations with Belgrade. But, as you know, it takes two to tango.” GEOPOLITICAL SETBACK Russia can still count EU member Slovakia, under Prime Minister Robert Fico, as a friendly country. It has also been closely watching unrest in France, where far-right politician Marine Le Pen has said she would cut financial aid to Ukraine if she won next year’s presidential election. Recent regional electoral successes for the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) have been welcomed in Russia, where Mr. Putin’s special envoy Kirill Dmitriev has begun to speak about the possibility of one day reopening the Nord Stream gas pipelines between Germany and Russia which were blown up in 2022. But for now at least, the potential loss of Serbia as a close ally — after setbacks to Russia’s geopolitical influence in the South Caucasus region and parts of Central Asia — is being seen as a serious blow in Moscow by Kremlin-aligned politicians, media and analysts. Before Sunday’s election, the Student List party said it would not introduce sanctions on Russia over Ukraine, that it would retain Serbia’s military neutrality, and that it would not seek to join NATO. Mr. Vucic has cast doubts on those pledges, suggesting the party would renege on them and impose sanctions on Moscow as soon as March or April. Jovo Bakic, a representative for Student List and university lecturer, on Monday denied his party would U-turn. “We respect Russia both as a great power and as our historically important partner and, in many cases, protector. There will be no changes there (in the country’s foreign policy),” Mr. Bakic told Russia’s RT Balkan TV outlet. Members of Russia’s political elite fear Serbia’s EU aspirations could see it put under serious pressure to align itself more closely with EU foreign policy however and that Moscow could find itself betrayed by a traditional ally in the process. “Brussels, for its part, is keen to see Belgrade align itself more closely with the common European position on Russia. The main indicator of Serbia’s actual course will not be Vucic’s statements or his opponents’ electoral pledges, but rather the first decisions taken by the new cabinet,” said the Moskovsky Komsomolets newspaper. Fyodor Lukyanov, editor-in-chief of the influential Russia in Global Affairs journal, said it was clear that a new political era was under way in Serbia that could sharply reorient the country towards the EU, in the same way that Mr. Orban’s loss of power in Hungary saw Budapest and Brussels become much closer. “In this sense, the Hungarian case is quite telling,” said Mr. Lukyanov. “And Russia has nothing good to look forward to.” — Reuters LATEST NEWS Paraguay widens probe into collapsed digital bank and installs new central bank head November 10, 2026 | 9:02 am Typhoon Cempaka exits PAR amid northeast monsoon November 9, 2026 | 9:34 pm Philippine economic slowdown deepens in Q3 November 9, 2026 | 9:29 pm Debt-to-GDP ratio hits 66.9%, highest since 2004 November 9, 2026 | 9:28 pm Job shortage risks wasting skills of Filipino graduates November 9, 2026 | 9:27 pm BSP eyes polymer banknote production in 2027 November 9, 2026 | 9:26 pm DoE sees jumbo rollback in gasoline prices of at least P16 a liter this week November 9, 2026 | 9:25 pm Marcos expands school counseling, promotions November 9, 2026 | 9:24 pm Speaker Dy orders review of 2026 projects; House readies budget portal November 9, 2026 | 9:23 pm Witness can’t link Duterte SALN to property November 9, 2026 | 9:22 pm Top News Paraguay widens probe into collapsed digital bank and installs new central bank head Typhoon Cempaka exits PAR amid northeast monsoon Philippine economic slowdown deepens in Q3 Debt-to-GDP ratio hits 66.9%, highest since 2004 Job shortage risks wasting skills of Filipino graduates
